utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Moric, I would like to remind you, as I did before, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to continue your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moric. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will have several more questions before completing my re-direct. Mr. Moric, a very brief topic, cooperation with UNCIVPOL. You were shown the agreement signed by Mr. Sarinic and Mr. Akashi, which addresses the powers of UNCIVPOL with regard to contacts with the police. At the ministry level, did you receive any reports or complaints or any sort of documentation from UNCIVPOL which would relate to the cooperation I've just referred to or any other matters?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, in the early days, during the peacekeeping operation, contacts with UNCIVPOL had to do with cooperation and arrangements aimed at implementing this sort of cooperation. There were letters exchanged to that effect. If you're asking me whether we received any reports on specific security-related incidents, then the answer will be no, not at the level of the ministry but at the lower levels of police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we call up document 2D180331.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, pursuant to the rules governing the joint activities of the police and UNCIVPOL, and this is D53 for Their Honours' reference, Mr. Elleby, who was the commander of UNCIVPOL sent a memo to UNCIVPOL members, indicating the procedure that they should follow in their contacts with the police in the newly liberated areas. What we see on our screens is not the document, and my Case Manager has just told me that the document I've asked for has already been admitted into evidence, and that's D1751, and the page should be the next page of the document that we have on our screens now. It's the 30th of August document from the Ministry of the Interior signed by the chief of the police sector, Mr. Franjo Djurica, where he sends the rules governing the joint work of the MUP and UNCIVPOL in order to ensure uniformity of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we turn to the next page, please. We have it on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where, under item 1, it is stated that in formers Sectors, North and South, UNCIVPOL will be monitoring the work of the police but only in regard to the protection of human rights. Further down in item 7, it is stated that UNCIVPOL members can observe the work of the police --

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have item 7 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the next page in Croatian. UNCIVPOL members would be observing the work of the MUP and note the observed, but not with audio or videotapes. Mr. Moric, do you recall any specific problems in the police work when it came to on-site investigation? Had you ever heard of any problems in that regard during crime-scene examinations, in cooperation -- problems in cooperation with UNCIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the level of the ministry, did you receive reports from the UN HRAT, Human Rights Action Team?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't recall receiving them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we have the documents on our screens, the one which was sent by Chief Djurica on 30th of August, let us move on to a different topic, that of coordinators and their rotation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To that end, can we please move into private session for a moment, and let's look at P487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric, in your line of duty, you attended numerous meetings at the level of the ministry and in contacts with the military police administration. Had you ever been informed at these meetings about a security-related legal problem related to the special police? Had you ever been told that their conduct might have been tied in with any of the crimes that emerged in the wake of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall having been informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, in the ministry or your office receive a report or a complaint about the conduct of the special policemen?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither my personnel nor I ever received that sort of report or complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, at that time or immediately after 1995, any of the special policemen were the subject of a criminal report or criminal charges, in relation to the crimes committed in the newly liberated areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only recall such cases existing in the civilian ordinary -- uniformed police, which disappointed me greatly. But I don't recall there ever having happened something of the sort you described in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Kehoe, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President this will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, yesterday during the course of your examination, you asked to make a comment on your order of the 18th, which is D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could bring it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is your order of the 18th concerning what you were doing concerning check-points, moving ahead with other investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just bring that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, again, we're referring to paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Moric, you were being questioned on the legality or illegality of this order, and you said you wanted to make further comment on that issue, and I give you the floor at this point to make further comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, the order is fully in keeping with the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs. The Law on Internal Affairs, which, I believe, was tendered into evidence by Mr. Mikulicic, provides in no uncertain terms, in Article 10, if I'm not mistaken, the competence and responsibilities of the Ministry of the Interior. In other words, of the state itself, in relation to the general state of affairs with regard to -- to security matters in the state. It also provides that the ministry shall monitor the state of affairs an events related to security and take measures in order to implement the legislation. The responsibility thus conferred by the law has been also set forth for the police administrations -- and police administrations in almost the same terms. In this way, the competence and responsibilities of every organisational structure of the police in the country has been legally defined or defined in the law. On the one hand, this provides for the stability of the security system; and, on the other, it provides for an obligation to act proactively and retroactivity at all three levels. What this means, in practice, is that if the higher level makes an assessment with a considerable degree of certainty, to the effect that the lower level has failed to monitor the developments and the state of affairs or to take measures or that it has failed to take sufficient measures in order to ensure the enforcement of the law, the higher level has to react, either proactively or reactively. This system has provided for a clear terms defining the responsibility, in relation to the implementation of the legislation. I held the position of assistant minister of the interior in charge of uniformed police. I was a state official, a civil servant who conducted his duties from this third level, as provided for in the Law on Internal Affairs. Just as the law dictates, I monitored the state of affairs and the developments; and, based on reports, I took decisions on measures to be taken in order to implement the law. This did not have to do solely with the territories liberated by Storm but with the entire country. My proactive activities had to do with the preparations of 3.000 policemen, who were seconded. I think the number in the transcript is wrong, I'm sorry. I said around 3.500 policemen who were seconded to the police administrations in the liberated areas. In doing so, I exposed the state border and the critical infrastructure to high-security risks; and, unfortunately, the infrastructure had been the frequent target of terrorist activities subsequently, since terrorists had crossed the state border with large quantities of explosives and aimed their terrorist attacks against the railway lines, the motorways, and these facilitates at places that were 160 kilometres away from the closest area affected by Storm. In doing so, I exposed to the high-security risks around 4 million inhabitants of the country because the rate of crime increased to their detriment. Let me not belabour the point by expounding on the risks that we exposed ourselves to by deploying these 3.500 policemen. I will only concentrate on the liberated areas. I also monitored the situation in these areas. From the reports that I insisted on receiving, as we were able to see in the various documents, whenever I was dissatisfied with the precision of these reports, I insisted that they be re-written. These reports enabled me to understand that the police stations located in these areas did monitor the situation but failed to take sufficient measures to implement the law. I also came to realise that the police administrations, whilst monitoring the situation, did not take sufficient measures to implement the law. I consulted experts on my team and chiefs of police administrations. I alerted them to the fact that they had more than 500 of their own policemen and around 3.500 seconded policemen, that they had 4.000 out of the total of 11.000 policemen in existence across the country. I cautioned the military police. I cautioned my minister about the many facts and difficulties which prevented the police from implementing measures it was bound to implement under the law. I asked that courts be reinstated in the area, because at the time there were neither criminal nor in misdemeanour courts. I described the situation in the area, in the course of my testimony here, as a post-war area riddled with confusion. I realised that new security risks must not be allowed to threaten us in the remainder of the Republic of Croatia or in the areas liberated by Storm. I found myself in a delicate situation. What else could be done to change the tactics of police work so as to enable us to yield better results? To improve our performance. This is what I decided and informed my associates and ministers of. I drew their attention to priorities that had to be strictly implemented, in keeping with the law. In Article 2 or Article 3 of the Law on Internal Affairs, tasks to be performed by the police are listed in a -- in a certain order. The first task is the protection of life. The second, protection of property, of all persons as a universal category, of all people as a universal category. The third task, crime prevention. The fourth, detection of perpetrators. Other tasks are listed as well, which are less relevant for the topic. The order in which these priorities are listed in police work is not a coincidence. It is inherent to the very nature of police work. In peacetime, the police deals with all these tasks that were listed at once, regardless of the order in which they appear. However, even then - and this is something that is clear in all the police systems around the world - the protection of life, property, and crime prevention are the primary tasks. That is why every police force would have several-fold more personnel of the ordinary uniformed police than the other police branches of the Ministry of Interior. Faced with a spate of attacks on the lives and property of citizens, and primarily abandoned property, I understood, or realised, that we could not be doing our job in such a way as to have the best performance at the same time in all these different types of work. That's why I sent an order to the police, asking them to focus all of their attention on the first three priorities within the law, and let me remind you what they are. They are the protection of life, protection of property, and crime prevention. The fourth priority after that is detection of perpetrators. That was the main reason why I decided to do so. The reason was to protect the lives of the people who had stayed behind, to protect their abandoned property. I wanted all of us to concentrate on the job at hand. I did it deliberately and intentionally. I took a deliberate risk, knowing that sooner or later I would have to explain my actions, although the actions were based on the provisions of the law. Fortunately enough, that was a successful attempt to change the tactics of the police work. And let me -- let me illustrate this by saying that I wanted my police officers to use surgical precision in order to focus on a problem that was the topmost priority at the time. I have gone at a very great length. However, I believe that Madam Prosecutor quoted from Mr. Cetina's testimony, and she said that he had doubts about the legality of my decision and of my document, and she asked me if I was surprised. And my answer to that was that I was, indeed, surprised, and that was an understatement. Mr. Cetina was the chief of the Zadar and Knin police administration. At the time when he received this document, under the rules that were in effect at the time and that regulated the mutual relationships among the police employees, he was obligated to the warn me, to draw my attention to the fact that he had doubts about the legality of my document. He didn't. Moreover, in his report that he submitted on either the 23rd or the 24th, and the document, if I'm not mistaken, was tendered for admission by Mr. Kehoe last week, Mr. Cetina informed me that, from the 18th of August, which was the date when this document took effect, there was a -- a significant decrease in the number of attacks against abandoned property. And, finally, not only was this document founded in the obligations of the Ministry of the Interior to monitor the situation and developments and to take measures with a view to implementing the law, this document of mine dated the 18th of August also contains a very clear judgement on the work of the police administration, and it says that they did monitor the situation and the development, but they did not do enough. They didn't take enough measures to implement the law, which is why the third and the highest level, which is the state, had to step in, in order to safe-guard the security in the area. In their reports in which they admit that changes in the police work tactics resulted in the improvements, they admitted that I was right. There's no reference in the document of the 18th of August to the fact that the police would never have to deal with crimes that had taken place before the 18th of August. It arises from the very context of the document, that the police would have to continue dealing with those crimes. And, finally, thousands of criminal reports that were filed clearly show that those criminal reports were also filed for those crimes that had taken place before the 18th of August, and the reports were filed much later than the 18th of August. I'm convinced, I was convinced then and I'm still convinced, that we did a good job and that our work was based on the provisions of Articles 10 and 2 or 3 of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no questions of Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the reference of the Chamber, the document is D1077. It's a Law on the Internal Affairs and it's Article 1 and Count 2 of which Mr. Moric was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I wanted to ask you several questions regarding different subjects. And the first is the Chamber received some evidence indicating that Mr. Cermak issued several orders addressed to Knin police administration regarding stolen UNCRO vehicles for instance, freedom of movement, securing entrances of UN compound and to investigate specific crimes. As a general understanding was the police actually act in accordance with this -- these orders? Did you ever, being as assistant of minister, ever receive from the President or government authorities written or oral instructions concerning how police should cooperate with Mr. Cermak? And did you personally instruct either of writing, or verbally chiefs of police administrations as they should cooperate with Mr. Cermak, and whether the police obliged to execute Cermak's orders and report back to Cermak?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, irrespective of the state of turmoil which existed at the time, and politicians could talk, as they would, but I can tell that you I never received a written order from the office of the President of the state, from my government, or from my -- indeed, my minister which would show that Mr. Cermak had any authorities over the civilian police. Yesterday when Madam Prosecutor examined me and showed me that pass that either Mr. Cermak or his staff were supposedly going to issue, I told her that, when I saw that, I was very angry. But I also said that I had not seen the document that the protected witness dispatched with regard to that idea about the passes, because if I had seen the document, if I had known about it, then that particular protected witness would be charged with disciplinary responsibility within the system that he acted within. Under the Law on Internal Affairs and based on the factual situation, in view of the way my associates and I managed the police system, Mr. Cermak did not have access to at that system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But how you would explain that actually police obeys these orders and conduct in accordance with this information? Secure, for instance, gates; there was also a question regarding these passes, just only this expectation with Mr. Cipci, and another situations?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, police receives information about security problems in an area in all sorts of ways from all sorts of citizens. I personally believe that the document that Mr. Cermak sent to the police were understood as information about the problem. And when it comes to providing security for certain objects or facilities that Mr. Cermak requested and the police complied with his request, obviously there were some security reasons found by the police which mandated for the facilitates to be secured. In a situation, as I have just described it, it would not have been sensible from a local police commander to use his human resources for unimportant things; let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: What it means that securing of graveyards, it is very important thing for police work? Restricting access to -- from international monitors to these areas.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there are security risks, and I don't know about any particular case. I can't remember. However, if there are security risks, as, for example, clearing minefields in or around such a graveyard, then, of course, it is mandated and important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: It is related only with burning of dead bodies, not -- not just finding mine explosives or whatsoever. Is it significant task for police, that police should act in accordance with such instructions?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about an ordinary burial without any security implications, then I don't see police playing a role in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: But actually Chamber receives evidence that such actions took place, securing Gracac cemetery, Knin cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, from my own point of view, from the point of view which was in position of managing police across the country, I provided you my very firm opinion as to when the police should have been present and when not. If there were reasons of the sort that I enumerated, then it is understandable that the police were present. If those reasons did not exist, then there is no reason why the police should have been present. If there are no security risks, then I don't know why the police should have been present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Last question would relate with following: The Chamber received evidence through either Kardum, indicating that a very low number of crimes committed in Knin area were reported to the Zadar-Knin critical police. Even through other evidence indicated that many international observers submitted information about ongoing criminality to the police almost every day. The Chamber also has received evidence indicating that in aftermath of Operation Storm sanitation teams including criminal police experts collected human remains by putting them into plastic bags, placing them on trucks, and taking them away. The Chamber has heard testimonies according to which sanitation teams simply collected bodies without any on-site investigations or securing crime scenes taking place. The Chamber also receives in evidence, for instance, the log-book of Knin police in which entries indicated that dead bodies are found in area, but where only indicate the action was that police send information to sanitation teams. Based on the above said, there might be some indications that such method is not -- not report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could please, Judge, could you slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Yes. "Based on above said, there might be such indications that such method and not to report to the criminal police about incidents committed in area, aftermath Operation Storm was conducted in planned manner." I'm looking at this in accordance with your order issued from 18th of August, because this order, actually paragraph 2 and 4, indicates that what actions should be taken afterwards. Could you give, please, some explanation of this.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, teams who were dealing with sanitation in the area were structured in compliance with the international standards prescribed by international conventions. On those teams there were also forensic technicians. Their jobs -- their job was to go to the sites and make an assessment as to whether there were any human casualties, and then start the procedure, be it a police procedure or the procedure of sanitation which was the humane disposal of human bodies. In cases that you have just described, as far as I know, forensic technicians identified victims, or if the identification was not possible, then they took samples for subsequent identification of the victims. Obviously, as you may well understand, I -- I don't know anything about their work in detail because they were not part of the operative police force. And as for your doubts, with regard to my document dated the 18th of August, and whether it could be construed in such a way, I believe that when you look at the document, Your Honour, you will be able to conclude that it could certainly not be applied to such cases, because in this document, there is no reference at all to attacks against human life. Attacks against human life and protection of life against such attacks are the first priority of the police work. In my document, there's no reference whatsoever to attacks against human life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Did anyone order such information should be just forwarded to the sanitation teams rather than investigated? And how could police, if they did not conduct an on-site investigation, distinguish between victims of military conflict and victims who died as a result of criminal activity? Were there any criteria for when an on-site investigation should be carried out; and when it was enough to forward information to sanitation teams?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for any special criteria of the kind, they don't exist in the police practice. A decision as to what course to take, unfortunately, is based on the assessment and competence of police experts, irrespective of the branch of the police force they come from. As far as I remember, in these particular cases, the prevalent opinion was the opinion of forensic technicians who were educated and who should have been able to make their assessment based on what they saw and conclude, whether they were dealing with victims of an aggravated crime or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that actually such method would also be used as some sort of cover-up?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in some particular cases, I suppose that this could have taken place. However, I exclude the possibility that, within the context, as such, as we had, and with the intentions that were clearly implemented that such a thing could have happened in an organised manner. What I'm saying is that there was no way somebody could have orchestrated the cover-up of some things, but I'm not excluding a possibility of something that happens, both in peacetimes as well as in the times of war that somebody made a wrong assessment. Therefore, I cannot exclude the possibility that somebody may have abused a situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: And last question for me is, the Chamber also received evidence indicating that police temporary confiscated different items, or the household items found in possession of certain civilians and placed those items under police control. However the Chamber also received evidence indicating that this did not always lead to initiation of criminal proceedings. My question is: Do you know what happened with those items, if criminal proceedings were not initiated? And did the police return those items, or were they sequestered for the benefit of the state?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my country the police practice at the time, was that objects that were used in crime or the proceeds of a crime were seized pursuant to a procedure, and later on used in evidence. That was a standard procedure which was applied to such objects. Last year, in the course -- last week, in the course of my testimony, I described some situations that posed problems for the police, which largely depended on the type of objects and their numbers. However, if the true owner of the objects could not be determined for various reasons, or if a certain quantity of various objects could not be used in evidence in future proceedings or their owners could not be determined, there are a lot of such examples today, and there were at the time, and what happened to such objects or property was they were sent to public auctions or sold off, and the proceeds went either to the state budget or something of the sort. In any case, everything was done publicly. It was well known which objects were being sold and when, in a public auction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Did you have special instruction at that time how to deal with such -- such temporarily confiscated objects? How to register it, how to -- how to sell for auctions, or return to persons whom they were withdrawn, and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that instructions or specific directions existed, but they were not part and parcel of operative police work or of uniformed police work, and that's why I have no detailed knowledge of it and cannot give you a precise answer. These were matters dealt with by logistics and legal affairs departments of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Isn't there was such situations before departure of Knin -- of Split -- this railway, police just withdraw from -- from passengers huge amount of different items. And nobody could explain to us what happened with those items, because it's obvious that -- it's quite -- quite hard to understand that if persons were allowed to follow to go back home to Split and, again, somebody could criminal investigation initiated. It means actually that they were simply collected in one place, and what's happened after? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're referring to items which would, in actual fact, constitute evidence about an individual having committed a crime or having been in the process of committing crime, because in other cases the police would not be impounding items at all, if this was the case, then there was standard procedure in place which had to do or was connected with a report filed against the individual from whom the items were seized. I do not rule out the possibility that, unfortunately, some of the members of the police may have abused the procedure. In the course of my testimony, we had occasion to see that I had to deal with some situations that were a great disappointment to me. These were situations of which I was informed by Mr. Cetina, where several policemen were caught red-handed, committing crimes. We could also see from the documents shown during my testimony that I was monitoring the situation in that field as well as dictated by the law and that I issued special instructions, a special order as to how the police force was supposed to rotate and that special attention had to be paid in the rotation process to the attempts on the part of those who were leaving that area and going back to the area of their normal work duties, to carry along items that were not their belongings, and that there had to be disciplinary action initiated and suspension effected in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: I understood from your answer, actually, that all activities afterwards happened with those items who was withdrawn from persons, it is duty for logistic department or -- or legal department, what you mentioned but not for -- for general police. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fear that I may not have understood fully some of your questions. I think that we were at cross purposes speaking about two different matters. When dealing with items that had been seized as evidence, one type of procedure is envisaged, and where we are talking about items which clearly do not belong to the person on whom they were found, and thus indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm talking about the second type of items which were -- there is allegations that persons cannot prove that these items belong to them, that is why police withdraw from them. But there is no indications that criminal investigation followed. This is my question. What's happened with those items?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, it is clearer to me now. This second or latter category of situations where the owner cannot be found, a period of time is allowed to pass in case the rightful owner might show up. I think that the period was even specified, but I don't recall the time-limits. Upon the expiry of such a time-limit within which the rightful owner might appear, there follows something that we discussed already, a public auction which is duly announced in advance so that all those interested may appear. If I recall the procedure correctly or the principle underlying the procedure, the rightful owner could report shortly before or during the public auction. But this was a matter for logistics and legal affairs services and not the ordinary police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moric, for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, in your statement, you said, and I read it to you - there's no need to put it up: "Military commanders had no powers or competences over the civilian police. Such sporadic attempts by military commanders had no legal effect on the actions of the police." Could I ask you to give examples of what you refer to when you said "such sporadic attempts."

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was referring to situations where civilian police may be faced with some oral orders from military commanders at the levels of companies, regiments who would sporadically ask chiefs or heads of civilian police to get involved in an operative action which could be related to road traffic or similar situations. In these circumstances, the police would be acting preceding from military authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It -- especially the last part of your answer is not entirely clear to me. Would you say that in these circumstances the police would be or would not be acting under military authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a matter of judgement or assessment. I don't think that the police would do something only because asked to do so by a military officer. But I do not exclude the possibility that there were cases where some of the police staff, in full respect for the authority of military personnel, did something that they thought was purposeful or sensible to do at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would be in accordance with what these military commanders had asked them to do, or required to do, or ordered to do, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, if the case was such that the civilian police believed that the request had a purpose and made sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of such an occasion where this happened.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a specific case in point. I could draw upon a situation from real life and try and describe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your answer, you did not intend to refer to any orders given by Mr. Cermak, who was, at least formally, a military authority, orders given to the police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I was able to see the documents during proofing for my testimony, I can speak on the basis of what I saw when I was reviewing them, and I could use them as an illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would consider them examples of what you refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be an example. When I answered His Honour's question a moment ago about Mr. Cermak asking that security be provided for some of the facilities. Therefore, if the civilian police decided that it made sense to secure certain facilities, then it could have happened. However, it happened only if my staff and I were not informed. In the cases -- or had we been informed of that, it would most certainly not have happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that if what was asked, requested, ordered, suggested, whatever terms were used, to do something, that the police would consider whether it would be useful to act in accordance with such wishes, requests, orders, whatever. And you say if you would have been informed about that, that it would most certainly not have happened. Why not?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for my ineptness. Not in the form of a document which would state, I order. Had I been informed at the time of the police receiving documents stating, I hereby order, I would have requested the police to consider the document as a piece of information that may have come from any ordinary citizen; and, on the other hand, I would have alerted Mr. Cermak to address such information through the regular channels normally used by ordinary citizens when addressing the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the result may have been the same, that the action was taken as requested. I mean, if the order, which you say would not be an order that could be issued, that would, nevertheless, could result in a situation where the police would act in accordance with what was described in that document, if they considered that it would make sense.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with your formulation, if the civilian police believed that it makes sense. And this is something that would have to fit with the duties and responsibilities as provided for by the law. It would only make sense if it was compatible with these duties and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would chiefs of police or those in command over the police activities, would they know that they were supposed not to follow orders, for example, from Mr. Cermak, because he was not in a position to issue any orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to the responsibilities defined by the Law of the Ministry of Interior, on the one hand, and of the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Croatian Army, on the other, every civilian police officer is quite clear on the fact that the competence and responsibilities of these differ, and that there can be no overlapping under the law or there can be no mutual interference. In other words, interference with someone's competence and responsibility, or the very attempt at interference cannot happen, if it is to be in keeping with the law. However, I, myself, on one or two occasions found myself in a situation where - and I was doing a different job of work, it was a different time-period - there was some military documents which had to do with the activities in the area affected by Flash, and I was not consulted on the matter, and the results were next to none. So there were situations where, inadvertently or out of inept handling of a situation, the events would take an awkward turn. That's why the formulation contained in the law, whereby at every level, state of affairs and situations must be monitored in order for the law to be implemented. Hence, that formulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In a follow-up to one of Judge Kinis's questions, securing a graveyard, not giving access to members of international organisations, where there would have been an instruction, or a request, or an order, to secure that graveyard where you may find difficulties in understanding what purpose that would have served within the framework of the police duties, if such an order would, nevertheless, or such a request would, nevertheless, be implemented by the police, could you assist us in understanding why that would then have been the action taken? So I'm talking about situations where a request, order, whatever, in whatever terms would have been issued by a military authority, such as Mr. Cermak. And if it's really difficult to see what police purpose -- so, therefore, that the -- as you said before, that it's difficult to understand that it would make sense to do that. Could you assist us in understanding why, nevertheless, under such circumstances, the police would act in accordance with that request, order, whatever, as issued by the military authority.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the one in charge of the civilian police over a given area assesses that there are security risks of any sort, or for reasons that were provided for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm talking about the situation where the circumstances and the information is such that one could not identify any security risks or any other reasons which would result in it making sense to do what was asked, ordered. I'm talking about those situations. If, nevertheless, under those circumstances, the police acted in accordance with what was requested, or ordered, could you assist us in understanding why, then, that would have place -- why that, then, would have been the line of action of the police.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I regret that I cannot assist with this. I would not have acted in a situation as you described. But the answer to this question can only be given by the person in charge of a police force in a particular area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. I am -- Ms. Mahindaratne, is there any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of matters that arise from Your Honours' questions. They would probably be better dealt with after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give an assessment of how time approximately --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Under ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under ten minutes. Then I'm just wondering -- if it is under ten minutes, then perhaps we could have a late break, and that we could then excuse Mr. Moric. But I'm also looking at interpreters and all others assisting us whether we would -- then I give five minutes extra break after that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, can I just clarify the last matter, concerning securing a graveyard. And the assumption was made that there could be no reasonable reasons why a graveyard would need to be secured, and you, yourself, said, I don't know of any reasons. You referred to mines, maybe security, and said you would need to ask the policemen involved. Can I put a scene to you that may, in fact, carry with it reasons for security. At the time of conflict, conflict between two people, Serbs and Croats, were there examples during the conflict when churches or religious buildings of the -- of other ethnic groups were liable to be attacked, damaged?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't realise that you have finished. Yes, there were such cases, the cases of attacks against churches, and, unfortunately, graveyards, and also burial ceremonies, unfortunately. However, Counsel, the Trial Chamber asked me this. If there is no reason, that's how they preceded their question, that's why I said that it is up to the person to answer that question, to that person who manages the police in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I understood why you gave the answer you did, because of the no reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay, just -- you said that was suggested. That it was put at the basis of the question. There was no suggestion that, under no circumstances, there could be any security concern at, for example, burials. That's not what was implied in my question. If that may be clear, do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I was just reading the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just deal with a couple of issues Judge Kinis raised with you because I think you answered half his question. He put to you specifically, did you ever receive from the President or government written or oral, verbal instructions on how the police should cooperate with Mr. Cermak? You replied written -- that you never received written instructions. Did you receive any oral instructions from the President or government?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I did not receive either written or oral instructions about the real or possible cooperation with Mr. Cermak. From the point of view of internal security matters, he was not an important player in the area, when it came to the matters of security in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just on another aspect of His Honour Judge Kinis's questions, again, he put it in a two-way. Did you instruct in writing or verbally police administrations should cooperate with Mr. Cermak and police report back to Mr. Cermak? So Judge Kinis was interested in whether there had been instructions in writing by you, verbally or in writing.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there were no reasons prescribed by the law for me to do so. There were no professional reasons either. Nothing whatsoever to do with the police and their tasks. Mr. Cermak was an outsider. Mr. Cermak was not capable of performing such tasks, and he did not have the authority to perform them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Kay was asking whether, where you answered the question about written instructions, that you intended to say that you gave no instructions at all, whether in writing or any verbal instructions. Is that what, Mr. Kay, what you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is, but I took from the terms of what the witness said and the language used by him that he answered it, Your Honour, unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you not only did not give any written instructions, but also no verbal instructions in this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's my final question, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Moric, this concludes your testimony. You have been with us for quite many days. Thank you for coming to The Hague. Thank you for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to thank you, and to the parties, to the personnel of the Tribunal who have taken care for me. I came here because that was my obligation. I had certain prejudices, but now I am leaving home without those prejudices. Thanks to you, Mr. President, to the Trial Chamber, and the way you work. Thank you very much, Your Honour. It has been my great honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn. And where the usual break is 25 minutes, at this point in time, we will resume now at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we -- yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was raising a matter I alerted the court's Chambers staff to, concerning the suggested bar table during my cross-examination of Mr. Moric, relating to documents concerning Knin 95. That bar table has been completed. It has been shown to the parties. It has been agreed. And what I suggest is if we can make the six documents that go into the table of those documents exhibits now, with the court's leave, we can then file it with the court with exhibit numbers instead of 2D numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, of course, we'll decide at the moment when we have looked at it and see whether the material is fit to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. There's no objection, Your Honour, from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But of course we also know that we haven't seen yet the sheet explaining, et cetera, so that's part of -- of course, and we've seen that recently we received a bar table submission clearly saying, This is what the one party says, that's what the other party says. Not to say that there is not doubt about that. But to decide on admission before we have seen the material and before we have seen the table attached to it, might be a premature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we MFI the documents then, Your Honour. This is our real concern, so that we can link collections to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the screen of the Registrar, it seems that he has something on the screen which is -- consists of six documents. Mr. Registrar, if you would identify the documents and MFI them, so that we will then receive the submission of these bar table documents with the MFI numbers referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2D00498 shall be assigned Exhibit D1877, marked for identification. Document ID 2D18-1197 will be assigned Exhibit D1878, marked for identification. 65 ter document 2D00679 will be assigned Exhibit D1879, marked for identification. 65 ter document 2D00298 shall be assigned Exhibit D1880, marked for identification. 65 ter document 2D00092 shall be assigned Exhibit D1881, marked for identification. 65 ter document 2D00395 shall be assigned Exhibit D1882, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we're waiting for your filing of the bar table submission. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Pardon me for interrupting, but I was going to replicate the same procedure employed by Mr. Kay with the bar table documents that I have discussed with my colleagues in the Office of the Prosecutor. And they have been 65 ter -- given 65 ter numbers 1D3035 through 65 ter 1D3044. And I would ask that we go through the same procedure with MFI numbers for those ten documents. Those ten submissions, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so we're talking about -- Mr. Registrar, I think if they are -- the numbers, the 65 ter numbers are in sequence --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we can attach numbers in a similar sequence, that was a bit different with Mr. Kay because that was not a sequential order of documents. Mr. Registrar, 1D3035 through 1D3044, would receive MFI numbers -- exhibit numbers to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The following exhibit numbers, D1883 through the exhibit number D1892, all marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. These nine numbers being assigned -- is that the -- are these the numbers that were already submitted in a bar table submission, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They have not yet been, Mr. President. I just conferred with my colleagues in the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you can refer to them under these numbers, and they have the status of documents marked for identification. Before we proceed with the next witness, Mr. Mikulicic, in cross-examination, in the recent past, some attention was drawn to the fact that the person interviewing the witness, where then the 92 ter statement was sought to be admitted, was Mr. Djurica Franjo. Now, for the next witness, we see the same person interviewing one of the witnesses. Is that the same Mr. Djurica Franjo, chief of the police action?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The very same person, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would like to receive, because there was a suggestion of -- at least that's how the Chamber understood it. There was some suggestion in it, whether it was appropriate or not to have -- to ask persons to take statements -- I'm not talking about assisting in doing research or -- but specifically focussing on taking statements, persons who may have played a role in relevant events at the time. And the Chamber would like to receive brief submissions by the parties on whether there would be any reason or whether there would be any thoughts about this being fully appropriate or being less appropriate or inappropriate. The question by the Chamber is more or less triggered by the cross-examination, and rather than developing our own thoughts on the matter, the Chamber would prefer to receive -- to receive submissions on the matter. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be more happy to response on any suggestions made by our learned friends from the Prosecution office that triggered that topic. And, of course, according to their suggestions or remarks, we will respond accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether that's the way in which we will approach the matter. So your suggestion is let the Prosecution give its views on the matter, and if there is anything which is in need of any response that you will give that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. They rise that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic was earlier on his feet than you were, Mr. Waespi. Therefore, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I rise on a very much related point, so I would move to have my point globally addressed and if we are going to do submissions on this. A similar situation arose with the Office of the Prosecutor's lead investigator in this case between September of 1995 and, I believe, up to 1998, an individual named Joakim Robertsson. Mr. Robertsson was a member of UNCRO in Zagreb before, during, and after Operation Storm in a, what the UN calls an information capacity, which I think, generally speaking, is an intelligence role, and on or about the 1st of September, three weeks after Operation Storm became OTP's lead investigator in this case coming straight from Zagreb in his role there to the OTP to work on this matter. The Court will recall from the cross-examination of General Forand Exhibit D339, which was a red line comparison of a statement taken by Mr. Robertsson in 1996 which had striking similarities to a report that Mr. Forand had prepared for internal purposes in the Canadian army. And we rise because whatever concerns arise with Mr. Franjo, I think, the same applies to Mr. Robertson's role, or earlier in this case, given his role in UNCRO in Zagreb, and so I would ask the leave of the Chamber that we address Mr. Robertson's role as well in terms of deciding the proper function of an investigator who was involved, in fact, with the events that are at issue in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I must admit that I do not have all the details on my mind immediately. Was there any statement taken by Mr. Robertsson, admitted into evidence under Rule 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Virtually every statement taken by OTP dated between 1995 through and including 1997 has Mr. Robertson's name on it. You will also recall, Your Honour, that - I don't recall which witness it was specifically - but there was a questionnaire that Mr. Robertsson had prepared in the fall of 1995 which he circulated to any potential or many potential witnesses in the case, so, yes, his name is on many statements that are admitted into evidence. We can, of course, as part of our submission try to list all of them. But General Forand's statement is one that immediately comes to mind, and again that's -- Exhibit D339 is the red line comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to look into the issue especially also as it relates to Mr. Robertsson. I recall in fact that Mr. Robertsson was on the witness list of the Defence. He certainly was never on our witness list. And whether he was indeed an investigator who took statements at that time, I need to look at it. I do recall having seen a memo from Mr. Robertsson, I think addressed to Mr. Kehoe in the earlier stages of the case addressing indeed issues about the case. So I can further explore that. In relation to Mr. Franjo, I think that is his last name, and also Mr. Anto Soljic, both played a role in taking witness statements and, indeed, during Operation Storm. I think it was important for us to point out in cross-examination that it needs to be transparent that these two gentlemen who interview a witness indeed played a role and have met with the witnesses. And since no other member of the Defence was present during these interviews, as I see from the cover pages, I think there is certainly an element of reliability of these witness statements will now become evidence -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems, Mr. Waespi, as if you are starting already to make submissions. But from what I heard until now, apparently Mr. Waespi considers it perhaps a relevant matter, whether persons which were involved in the events, I am -- taking part in events. I'm putting this in a very neutral way. Whether they were alone during such interviews or whether there were persons present also who did not have -- who have not played any role during the events, that may be an issue to be addressed. Another matter, which also may be relevant in this respect would be is, how close the subject matter of the interview was to the role of the person who took the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might be one of the issues to be addressed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it is. But the Chamber did not develop its thoughts on the matter and did not wish to do it, but since the matter implicitly has been raised in cross-examination, the Chamber thought that it would be wise to first give an opportunity to the parties to address the matter before developing any further thoughts on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see I have to choose now and then, Mr. Misetic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to follow up on what Mr. Waespi said. Mr. Robertsson indeed was on our witness list and we did wish to explore some of these matters with him, but as Mr. Waespi also knows, Mr. Robertsson was unreachable by us. And when we inquired with Mr. Waespi to obtain contact details, the Prosecution refused to provide us the contact details for Mr. Robertsson at his request, but I'm sure I have an e-mail to that effect, that Mr. Robertsson had told the Prosecution that did he not want the contact information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said a minute ago that it looked as if Mr. Waespi started already making the submissions, which I considered that he should not do at this moment, but I do see that in response to that, that you're following his example, which you are not encouraged to further do that. We can deal with the matter. You can make a -- you can express any thought on this, including factual circumstances, for example, if someone was involved and if someone is hired by another, could they shield such a person from investigations by the other parties? Might -- that's already the third thought that comes now to my mind in listening to you. You're free to address whatever matter you would like to do, which is related to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's all I rose for. So if I understand you correctly, we are allowed to address the issue of Mr. Robertsson in our submission? That's all I was rising --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If -- first of all, you're always free to make whatever submissions you think relevant. But I can imagine that this request or this invitation by the Chamber triggered an already existing need to express yourself on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- and the chamber is primarily seeking transparency and not to develop thoughts on matters where the parties are unaware that this implicit attention which was paid to the matter that we had forgotten about it, or that we have not heard it. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this cannot go without a reply. If we want to talk about transparency, the Prosecution had Mr. Soljic on its witness list, did not call him, and did not mention that fact to any of the witnesses who were cross-examined by them. Without a single shred of proof, they are engaging in character assassination of our investigators, and I think that is highly improper. If they had any proof, they could have provided it to us in a written submission instead of asking questions of witnesses in a one-sided manner. And I think that is very appropriate, in my view, to ask a witness if he knows that Mr. Djurica was on the Defence witness list when they know that Mr. Soljic was on their list. I think that is completely inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I intended to avoid is that we would immediately receive the submissions the Chamber was inviting the parties to consider to make. I noticed that, apparently, it's a matter which was on the minds of both parties and that it even has a little emotional impact. Let me just -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited to make submissions, and not the one party responding to the other but to make whatever submissions. And if there is any need then to further respond to anything submitted by one party by another party, then the Chamber will consider whether it would be appropriate to make a second round in this. What would be a time-frame in which we could receive such submissions? I'm waiting for the suggestion of the parties. The end of this week? Or would you need the weekend for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I would appreciate until Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In writing, I take it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would prefer to receive this in writing. Is that agreeable by the other parties? I'm fully aware that there is a lot of pressure, and there are time restraints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we were only consulting because obviously we have a significant hearing on Wednesday that we are preparing for, but we believe we can get it done by Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By Tuesday ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one party says until Tuesday, which I understand to be close of business Monday. The other parties get it done by Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My issue with that, Your Honour, is that they're raising this issue of this supposedly being improper. I don't know what I'm supposed to respond to. I would like to know what I'm supposed to respond to. If they are claiming that these investigators of ours have done something improper or there is impropriety, I have nothing to respond to, other than to say that it is our opinion that there is nothing wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The primary issue whether in general terms, not whether someone did something inappropriate, but whether it is appropriate to invite someone to take statements on events to which he has been close himself. That is the issue, at least the Chamber, raised. And, first of all, to start with, in general terms, that's the issue. And not to say that the statement was in any way inaccurate or whether from a professional point of view that it's -- whether it's appropriate or it's preferable to avoid, or whatever you would like to raise. It may be clear to the parties that there are rules for counsel not -- if you have your own interest in a certain matter, you should refrain from dealing with that matter. Now, that's a rule which is applicable for counsel, and you could discuss such a rule in very general terms. Not to say that if I would have an interest as counsel in a certain matter that I would behave inappropriately, but whether there are risks involved in that, which better should be avoided, or should be avoided, or would preferably be avoided. I mean, that's the level at which the Chamber at this moment is seeking -- at least the Chamber was seeking the assistance of the parties. But from the exchange, it turned out that there may be a reason to address certain very specific matters in this case already at this stage. And I think my response to Mr. Misetic was that if there was any such thing, that he would not be prevented from raising that matter in this context. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the Markac Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would -- no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Drazen Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vitez, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text will now be handed out to you. Could you please make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I was informed that there may be a problem with your microphone. We'll carefully monitor whether we hear every word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If need be, I will move, Your Honour, if that is it necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, you will be examined -- you will first be examined -- I hear the problem. Mr. Vitez, you will first be examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic. And Mr. Kuzmanovic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to move, just to avoid the further problems. Might as well do it now. Better? Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, before we proceed I have a binder to make things easier for the witness for documents. May I please have the usher give the binder to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: My name is Drazen Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what your current occupation is.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I still work in the Ministry of Interior. I am the deputy of the head of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, our conversation obviously is transcribed and we have interpreters, so I will do my best to talk slowly so that the interpretation can come to you, and I will also wait for your answer so we don't talk over each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have 65 ter 3D00888 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, shortly on the screen will come your witness statement. Do you recall giving a statement to the Defence team from Mladen Markac, Mr. Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. I did provide my statement to the team. Mr. Ante Soljic and Franjo Djurica called me, and they introduced themselves as being members of the Markac Defence team, and I also already knew that. And they asked whether I would voluntarily appear as a witness in the case, which I confirmed, and we arranged a time when I would provide my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, I observe a slight inclination to give answers which go well beyond the question. The only thing you were asked whether you recall that giving a statement. You give a lot of details. If Mr. Kuzmanovic is interested in hearing further details, he will certainly ask for it. I think a simple "yes" would have answered the question completely. Please proceed, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page of this document, please, in both Croatian and English. Mr. Vitez, you see there on the last page, is that your signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And this was an interview that was conducted on -- on 12 May of 2009, and you signed the statement on 12 May 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, have you had a chance to review the statement that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And other than a correction which we'll address, does the statement accurately reflect what you told the members of the Markac Defence?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you gave this statement, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. I based my statement on my recollections, and I did tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I asked you the same questions today in court that you were asked prior to signing your witness statement that's on the screen before us, would you provide the same answers today in court as you did to the questions that were posed to you during the course of the interview that led to the statement, subject to the change that you made in paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please -- Your Honour, I'm going to move that we tender this document into evidence. I will address the supplemental information sheet separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Need that to be filed separately, or is it just a matter of correcting the statement and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's just a matter of correcting the statement, Your Honour. I will just pull it up, and then maybe I'll move to tender the statement after the supplemental is discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean is the change such that we need another exhibit number, or is it just a matter of correcting a small detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a small detail, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... because if we can deal with that, the date, and then there's no need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we go to paragraph 7, Mr. Vitez, of your statement. We will address the correction in this way. You had signed yesterday a supplemental information sheet after our meeting for preparation. And you noted that on the last sentence of paragraph 7, where it states: "On 9 August 1995, we handed over our positions ..." You wanted that to be corrected to be: "8 August." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see you nodding yes, if it is translated. Could you please pronounce your answer, because the record --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to change this, because it was a mistake. My unit left Gracac on the 8th, in the evening, or, rather, during the night on the 8th. Or rather, not from the area of Gracac but from the area of Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I've no objection to the statement coming in and just note, and I think you have issues before, that I probably have an earlier version of the English translation. There's just a couple of things which are different, but I take it the substance hasn't changed, and perhaps when I quote from the statement during my cross-examination, we will find out whether I have a proper English copy. The one I am working for is 2D04-1872.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We provided the OTP in September with the official translation that we received from the CLSS, so I can't tell you right now -- there is no substantive change to the statement so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. -- the number Mr. Waespi used is that -- that's not one which was uploaded, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One that is officially uploaded as the official translation is not the number Mr. Waespi provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, under those circumstances, I take it that we have uploaded the most recent version as far as the translation is concerned of the document. Mr. Waespi, if you would verify that, I take it. And since there's no objection against admission, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D1893. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1893 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would this be an appropriate time to read a summary of the witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Kuzmanovic. You have explained to Mr. Vitez the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: During Operation Storm, Mr. Vitez was assistant commander of the special police unit of the Varazdin police administration. Shortly before Operation Storm, Mr. Vitez's unit was ordered to take up positions at Mount Velebit. As part of the preparations for the offensive, he and other unit commanders attended a meeting in Stari Grad on the 3rd of August, where they received specific tasks related to the operation and were ordered to adhere to international laws of war, as well as to proper treatment of the civilian population and their property. On the 4th of August, when Operation Storm began, Mr. Vitez's unit broke through the first lines in the Mali Alan area in the Velebit mountains where they encountered ARSK forces and heavy resistance.
