They further advanced towards Gracac. On the 5th of August, the unit reached the entrance to Gracac where they remained in nearby Stikada during the 6th of August, without incident. On the 7th of August, his unit was ordered to proceed to Bruvno, and from there they proceeded to Donji Lapac. His units did not come in contact with ARSK forces from Bruvno to Donji Lapac. His unit remained in Donji Lapac in the outskirts until the afternoon when the Croatian Army arrived in the area. On the 8th of August, his unit was instructed to advance toward Kulen-Vakuf, and on the same day, his returned to base in Varazdin, Croatia. That is the statement [sic], Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, can you tell the Chamber, please, a bit about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I have a masters degree in economics. My area of specialization is management. And before that I obtained a university degree from the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber about your work in the police, when you began, up through the time of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I joined the police in 1980. That's when I enrolled in the secondary school for police officers, which I completed in 1984. I worked in the area of Dogava [phoen] Selo as a patrol police officer on the highway. And on the eve of the war in Croatia, I asked for transfer. I wanted to go to the area of the police administration of Varazdin. Soon thereafter, I became a member of the special police unit of the Varazdin police administration. I became a special police officer. After that, I became a team leader, an instructor after that, and then in 1997, after the war, my commander was retired, and I took over the unit. However, it only lasted for a short while, for a year maybe. And then pursuant to a ministerial decree I became the chief of the crime police in the administration of Varazdin. I stayed in that position for two years. And then in, 2000 pursuant to a ministerial decree, I became the chief of the police administration of Varazdin. I stayed in the position until the year 2008. And then the minister ordered me to take the post of deputy head of police at the Ministry of Interior, and this is the position that I am still in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, before we get into the activities before Operation Storm and through your participation in Operation Storm and afterward, could you explain to the Chamber what your role is currently. What -- what job function you have. You have explained the title, but can you explain to the Chamber what you do in that function.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: My office is run by the head of police, who has two deputies. I'm one of them, and I cover the border police, the uniform police, the intervention police. I also cover the work of the police academy, as well as the operations and communications centre of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please pull up D540.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, I am going to direct your attention to a document that's in evidence already, which was directed to the chief of the Varazdin police administration, dated July 22nd of 1995. Are you familiar with this order signed by Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This was an order that requested the special police from Varazdin to go to the -- report to the head of the Zadar-Knin police administration, to work with the joint forces of the special police; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you a part of that unit that went to Sepurine by the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I was a member of that unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us when you got to the area of Sepurine what happened next, as far as your unit was concerned. Up until the meeting in Stari Grad, which we'll refer to in a separate question.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: As we arrived in the territory of the police administration of Zadar and Knin, we established contact with members of the special police, and they transferred the entire formation consisting of some 140 men to the territory of the Sepurine military camp. There was some other units there together with us. We had our first meeting with General Markac, and we were given information that the enemy army -- or, rather, that they had indications that the enemy army might want to cut off the road leading from the bridge in Maslenica, which was the only connection between the northern and southern parts of Croatia, to Biograd Na Moru, that was the narrowest area of separation, and it was assumed that the enemy might attempt to break through in order to break communication between the northern and southern parts of Croatia. That's where we carried out patrols. Everything was ready, we prepared ourselves over the couple of days, and then information reached us that the danger no longer existed. And then we headed towards Stari Grad. And then we had a briefing on the eve of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you based before the meeting in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: At the Sepurine base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Stari Grad, and you talk about that in paragraphs 2 and 3 of your statement, can you explain what happened when you went to Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I went to Stari Grad together with my commander. We were supposed to attend a meeting that was called by Mr. Markac, all the commanders of special police units were there, and received concrete tasks. We were briefed as to what to expect. We were given our axis of action or directions of actions. We were told what was the main axis of attack and the units that would there. That was my unit for Varazdin. On our right was a unit from Split. And on the far right, there was a special police unit from Zadar and Knin administration that was in the direction of Tulave Grede. We received maps and directions, and after that General Markac addressed us and shared with us the intelligence gathered by our intelligence and operations teams. We were told what to expect. We were briefed about the enemy strength, their armament. And a special emphasis at that meeting, as at many meetings that we had with the General before, any operation was put on the behaviour of members of the special police in dealing with prisoners of war, the civilian population. And, in this particular case, given the fact that in the area that we were supposed to enter, there were also UN -- or, rather, UNPROFOR forces deployed there, especially emphasise was put on the fact that we were not supposed to touch their bases. We were not supposed to open fire on them. We were, rather, supposed to approach them, explain who we were. We were supposed to tell them that we were the Croatian Army, that we could extend all assistance that they might need, and they may be assured that there will be no danger for them coming from the Croatian force. Then we went back each to our unit, and during the night between the 3rd and the 4th, since we were at the level of the sea and there were a lot of unit there, during the afternoon and during the night -- or, rather, before 1900 or 2000 hours that evening, my special police unit managed to reach the height of 1400 metres above the sea level, and that's where we prepared ourselves for attack. We had another meeting with the complete unit. We conveyed to them what was expected from them, how were they supposed to fight and engage, and what behaviour was expected on their part. We conveyed to them everything that General Markac had told them -- told us about the civilian population, their property, the UNPROFOR forces, and their behaviour, and what was expected from them. And after that, we were in a carsed area -- or, rather, wooded carsed area, that's where we were during the night awaiting the morning, and awaiting for the beginning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, it is only now that the French translation was able to translate your words. Could you please slow down. At the same time, I saw Mr. Misetic was already on his feet a while ago. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a transcript issue. Page 53, it is line 17 on my LiveNote. The witness mentioned a town. It's southern parts of Croatia to, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, can we just take that up. You talked about to cut off the road leading from the bridge in Maslenica, which was the only connection between the northern and the southern parts of Croatia to ... and then you mentioned, apparently a geographical thing. Could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the bridge by Maslenica which connected the northern part of Croatia with the southern part of Croatia, and we were deployed all the way down to Biograd Na Moru.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Biograd with an "I," I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This -- Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a brief suggestion. For me, it's not clear what the witness's function was. I know he was the assistant commander of the special police in Varazdin, but the D540 was addressed to the commander. So is Mr. Vitez the commander of this unit, or is he still in an assistant function? That would be helpful, I think, for people to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take that Mr. Waespi would like to receive this information in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, I think we had this morning an all time record high, seven pages of an answer. The question what happened then may well lead to very lengthy answers. If could you keep a bit more control and to focus on what exactly you would like to know. I know that, of course, in-chief leading may an issue, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. I didn't want to lead the witness. I just wanted to let him explain things in his own words, but I'll make sure -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you please try to focus the attention of the witness to what you find most relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Vitez, if you slow down, we can catch every word you say. If you speak at the speed you developed a minute ago, then we might miss some of your words which would be a pity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, you heard the comment of my friend Mr. Waespi about D540. First of all, did you see D540 in your function at the time, the Croatian version of D540?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that version. It was shown to me by my unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time of the events when that order came to Varazdin, what was your function and capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vitez, I'll try to break down my questions so you can still answer them - and obviously in your own words - but in maybe shorter increments. You have led us up through Stari Grad, the meeting, and up to your climbing into Mount Velebit. Could you please explain to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, why don't we pull up P1237, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The cover page of this document, Mr. Vitez, is signed by you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of this document, please. You have already described in the second paragraph about your unit positions on the 3rd of August up in the Velebits. There are -- there is another paragraph following that says: "We received several pager messages during the night and would like to mention own two of them." And it mentions conduct in the operation according to international conventions, and that you received reinforcements. Do you recall what the other -- you mentioned two of them. Do you recall what the other pager messages referenced?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Do you mean reference being made to new men who joined the unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: My question wasn't clear. The paragraph starts: "We received several pager messages during the night and would like to mention only two of them." Were there other pager messages that you received; and if so, what were they, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I don't remember the other. I know that they came during the night. The first one was about the treatment of human civilians and their property and the respect for the international laws of war. And the second arrived maybe a year [as interpreted] before our engagement informing us that the enemy forces had just been reinforced by 120 new men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think on page 59, line 4 -- the second arrived how much time before your engagement?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: The second one -- no, actually, the one that cautioned us about conduct came right after midnight. And the other one, the reinforcements came perhaps an hour before our engagement, sometime at 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vitez. The transcript said a year before our engagement, so I just wanted to make that clear. You were talking, Mr. Vitez, about receiving intelligence information. Could you describe for me from whom the special police received its intelligence information, regarding position of the enemy and strength and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Most of the intelligence received came from our internal control. They had the task of gathering intelligence data about the enemy that we were supposed to engage, their strength, their weapons, their weak points, sections of their line that would be the most easiest to breach, and, of course, they were in coordination with the military services and the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, given your experience as a chief of police of the Varazdin police administration and your long-time service as a special police member and assistant commander, can you tell the Chamber whether or not the inner control branch of the special police had anything to do with discipline?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Do you mean the inner control branch that was under the special police sector or the office for inner control under the minister's competence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, why don't you explain to us the role of the first, and then can you explain to us the role of the second, if you can answer those.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I will do my best. In brief, the inner control office, which was attached to the minister's office, was tasked with covering the work of all the employees of the Ministry of Interior. That's to say, monitor their work. They monitored the work of both authorised and unauthorised personnel. They monitored the legality of everyone's work. They acted on anonymous reports we received from citizens at large, which could have to do with abuse of office on the part of some of the personnel of the ministry, or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they initiated or launched every single case, and then followed through, whether it had to do with misdemeanour, breach of discipline, or criminal liability. The internal control of the special police sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, before we get there, the interpreter didn't catch a part of your answer. Mr. Vitez, if could you sit a little closer to your microphone. You said on page 60, line 13, they acted on anonymous reports we received from citizens at large which could have to do with abuse of office on the part of some of the personnel of the ministry, or ..." And that's where the interpreter couldn't catch what you said.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Or on the part of a manager who was a member of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were about to explain the role of the inner control of the special police sector. Please go ahead and do that.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: The role of inner control within the special police sector was, to my knowledge, to give an intelligence and operative briefing prior to an action. But not just prior to an action. For instance, at Mount Velebit where we deployed, the inner control personnel gathered intelligence on the enemy forces, on their strength, assets. They prepared all the maps prior to actions, but they did not solely engage in preparations for combat activities. Rather, when -- when a police administration engaged special police units as part of preparations for actions where certain criminal groups or individuals had to be apprehended and who had been dealing in drug trafficking, trafficking of people or arms, they would be the ones gathering intelligence about the nature of the persons involved, i.e., whether the persons were dangerous, whether the persons were armed, and whether they are likely to resist arrest. This was to ensure that the special police could prepare for such actions well and carry -- and have at their disposal appropriate resources or equipment, in order to avoid casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one question to close this loop, Your Honour, and then we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, we will going on a break here quickly. I just wanted to finish this topic. You've described the two roles of the two different, basically, inner control mechanisms. Can you tell the Chamber what role, if any, the special police internal control had with respect to either initiating, investigating, or dealing with disciplinary issues, within the special police?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No. The inner control branch didn't have anything to do with it. The person responsible for discipline within each and every unit was its commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kuzmanovic, I think your time estimate was one to two sessions. May I take it that examination-in-chief will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It will be less than two sessions, Your Honour. I hope to be done -- I'm looking at my outline. I hope to be done in about -- probably before the end of the day today, that we're done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would try to achieve that. We'll have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you may proceed, but I would like to inform the parties that the Chamber would like to receive the submissions we earlier talked about by Tuesday, noon. Which allows us still to read it on Tuesday afternoon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, we left off when you were on Mali Alan, which you describe in paragraph 4 of your statement. Now, in P1237, I think which think is still on the screen, you discuss in this -- or its discussed in this war path what your main first task was to liberate the route Mali Alan, Sveti Rok, Obrovac. Describe for the Chamber, please, what things you encountered and -- basically until the end of that first day of combat and what kind of combat operations you were involved in. And I will ask you further questions beyond that. But just -- right now, just focus on that first day of combat, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: On the first day, when we received the order that we should proceed to attack, the reconnaissance operative group, which was, as always, ahead of the unit with six scouts, and its commander and instructor, two explosive specialists gained access to the area, cleared the area of mines, anti-personnel mines, so that the rest of the unit might reach the area smoothly. At around 7.00 in the morning, the first combat engagement took place in the area of Vrcina. The enemy engaged us with infantry fire, machine-gun fire out of their pill-boxes. The unit -- our unit was at the foot of the elevation, and they had the upper hand being on top of the elevation in bunkers. They were made out of logs, as we were able to see later on. Logs on which piles of stone had been stacked. Our reconnaissance unit asked for our artillery support. The scouts who spotted the enemy guided our fire, in order to have as many precise hits as possible. Since we were some 200 or 300 metres apart, that's to say, that was -- that was the distance from the enemy, we wanted to make sure that our own artillery fire did not engage in friendly fire. The enemy opened artillery fire on us but did not inflict any casualties among our troops. However, our neighbouring, adjacent units did sustain casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second before you continue. Mr. Vitez, at the bottom of this particular exhibit which is on the screen, P1237, you state: "The unit practically battled for every rock at the Mali Alan pass." Could you describe the type of terrain that you were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: It's rugged terrain. Rocks that was not really trafficable easily. We were in an open area, and that made it very difficult to reach the enemy positions. Two of our special policemen were taken prisoner. One of them had an entry/exit wound in the lower leg. The other one was injured -- had injuries to his face and arms. That was Mario Sestak, the one who had his leg wounded; and Goran Bahun [as interpreted], who had slight injuries. There were two sorts of risk. If a shell didn't kill you, then fragment of rock would. It was difficult for us to advance, since we had to leave the rocky shelter and head for an open area, an open space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you asked for the terrain, and we now know all the details about whether the in and exits wounds were at the lower leg or the upper leg. That is apparently not what you were seeking. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, you were discussing on page 64, you said, line 16, two of our special policemen were taken prisoner, it was interpreted. Does that mean two were wounded?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: They were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vitez, in P1237, on the next page, please, after the capture of the Mali Alan pass, there were -- there was an aircraft attack on your position. Could you describe that, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: As for the aircraft, I'm afraid I don't remember much. I know that the Croatian air force aircraft rocketed their positions in the morning. Whoever wrote the report made a mistake, because I don't think our forces came under an air-strike. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vitez, then you move on in this report to Gracac in the morning. And there's noted BPP were put up in that village outside of Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just another matter of clarification. Mr. Kuzmanovic tells the witness, In your report; and the witness responds, Whoever wrote the report. So if it could be clarified who actually is the author. I know he signed the cover page of p1237, but I'm still not sure who was the drafter of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The matter is clear do you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, are you familiar with the contents of what's in P1237, this report, that came under your cover letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. I signed the memo, since I was chief of the Varazdin police administration at the time. It was my duty to forward the memo, and the report was written by the commander of my special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in terms of the report itself, you have familiarity with the issues that are discussed in this report from your involvement in Operation Storm, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We can go back to the section of this report where you enter the suburbs of Gracac, and BPP, it's noted barrier check-points were put up in that village. Can you describe to the Chamber what BPP means.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: BPP was short for combat check-point. It was taken up by the special police unit in order to protect themselves and to ward off attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we've heard testimony in this case about check-points on the roads that were manned by the police and/or the military police. Can you describe to the Chamber whether or not outside of these barrier check-points the special police had ever been engaged in holding check-points as it relates to traffic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in the area of Gracac, you were near Stikada; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. Stikada was the name of the entire area. And the settlement's name was Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we get into detail about Gracac, I would like to ask you a question about what you called the reconnaissance operative group. Could you please describe what that group was and what their function was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Every special police unit had its reconnaissance operative group which engaged in reconnaissance for the purposes of offensive actions of the special police. Every reconnaissance group was duly trained in how to gather as much intelligence or information on the enemy as possible, about the enemy's disposition, strength, and assets at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In these groups, were there any persons who were involved in directing artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Of course. There was scouts as members of the group who directed artillery fire. There were also explosive specialists, who cleared mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Moving on to Gracac, you passed through Gracac on your way to Bruvno; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when Minister Jarnjak came to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was present, together with my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you went to Bruvno, what was the reason for your unit to be ordered to go to Bruvno?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: The possible counter-attack of the Serbian army was the reason for it. And we were ordered to go and deploy in the area, in order to prevent them from attacking, or foil their attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you went through Gracac, what, if anything, did you observe about any damage to Gracac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we have a time-frame. Now we were in Bruvno, I think that was the 8th of August. Now we're going back to the 5th when Gracac was entered for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I think we can get that date. The 5th was the first day in Mali Alan. The 6th -- well, let the witness tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, if we can have your statement, I'll refer to your statement. You have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talks about the second day as far as Gracac is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day when you got to Gracac, in paragraph 4 you arrived at Gracac. And then on the 6th prepared for activities. And on the 7th went to Bruvno. Now, as you were going through Gracac from the area to Stikada until you got to Bruvno, what, if anything, did you observe in Gracac, as far as damage was concerned?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: What I can remember is damage. I saw several buildings that were destroyed. But as far as I remember, they had been destroyed a long time previously. There had been vegetation growing out of the ruins. I don't remember any other damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Bruvno or began in Bruvno on the 7th, what was your next task, once you got to Bruvno?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: As we arrived Bruvno, we received a task, and together with the units of Primorsko Gorinska, anti-terrorist unit Lucko, and the Gospic unit, we were supposed to go across Bruvno and Mazin to Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you had stated earlier that you had gone to Bruvno in terms of trying to prevent a counter-attack. When you got to Bruvno, was there such a counter-attack that occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No. There was nobody there. And there was no counter-attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you got to Mazin, did you see whether there was any resistance or any people at all in Mazin?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: There was no resistance in Mazin. I saw elderly persons, men and women, standing outside of several houses in Mazin. Our policemen explained to them that they should stay in front of their houses and that there would be somebody else arriving, ordinary police or somebody else, to pick them up. We proceeded on our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you ended up that same day in Donji Lapac; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. That same day, we reached Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And we've heard testimony from a witness that went along the asphalt road to Donji Lapac. You -- your unit did not take that road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No. As we ascended the winding road above Mazin, we were supposed to take a dirt road along, or through a wooded area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Chamber how you got from Bruvno until the outskirts of Donji Lapac? What methods of transportation were you using?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: For the duration of our advancement, we went on foot. We had one combat armoured vehicle that was there to protect us, and the vehicle could travel that road. As we reached the first households outside of Donji Lapac, we came under artillery fire. Naturally, we didn't know if it was enemy or friendly fire because we had not asked for any artillery support along our axis. The problem was that we weren't able to reach our special police staff. We weren't able to get hold of them, since we were in between two high peaks, and it was impossible to establish communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did that last, that artillery fire that that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Roughly half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: After the artillery fire was over, you went further onto Donji Lapac itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, we carried on towards Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You describe in paragraph 7 of your witness statement what happened when you were in Donji Lapac. Could you tell the Chamber briefly what happened when you met with the members of UNPROFOR in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: When we got to Donji Lapac, our commanders were joined by General Markac, who, together with us, tried to enter their camp, or their base. However, they were all manning their combat positions and bunkers because they didn't know who we were. When we introduced ourselves as the Croatian forces, one of their officers spread the news to all the rest who were in the base. All these UN soldiers leapt out of their bunkers. They were happy and hugging one another. We all got into their base and had a cup of tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you entered into the UN base at Donji Lapac, what did you observe in the town in terms of damage, if any?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: I observed two or three buildings in the very centre which were on fire, or, rather, smouldering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long -- how long was General Markac with you in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: General Markac was with us when we entered the base. We held a meeting with them. General Markac told them that we are -- were part of the Croatian armed forces, that there was an operation going on, that there would be further activities in the direction of the Bosnia-Herzegovinian border. He told them that they were save and if they needed anything that they could turn to us. And then he left the area because a group of the special report had already left Boricevac and was headed towards the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that action was already under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vitez, you spent the evening in the -- in and near Donji Lapac with your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, unequivocally, whether or not any members of the special police were involved in the burning of Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, you -- your unit went to the Boricevac-Kulen-Vakuf area. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Our unit arrived there. We were not engaged in attack. We were the reserve and support for those who had gone in the direction of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were there in full combat gear all day waiting possibly to be engaged, but that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were eventually ordered to return to Varazdin on that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. A meeting was held with the chief of the special police sector, Mr. Sacic, and all those units that had been involved in combat from day one were then released.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, your units returned straight to Varazdin. Can you tell us when you went back, did you go back through Gracac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No. We went back through Udbina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, after Operation Storm, did your unit take part in any mop-up operations? Meaning the Varazdin special police unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: No, we did not take part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to call up document 2D00282, please. Mr. Vitez -- that's a 65 ter number, sorry. The document that's coming up is from the Varazdin police administration. Do you know Mr. Ivan Zitnjak?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Zitnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now the date of this document is the 6th of August of 1995, Mr. Vitez, and obviously you were not in Varazdin at that particular time. But are you familiar with the subject matter that is contained in this particular letter and what the purpose of this letter was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: As for the contents of this letter, it says here that the police administration of Varazdin is expected to send assistance to Zadar which was only normal after the Operation Storm. All the police administrations which were not directly involved in combat were expected to assist those police administrations that were primarily in manpower or, rather, in civilian protection. We can see here that they were looking for forensic technicians, people who were able to carry out on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I please have a number for this document, I'd like do tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1894. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify something in the record regarding a question that I had asked earlier. And probably it is because the way I phrased the question on page 71, line 24, the question was: "Can you tell the Chamber, unequivocally, whether or not any members of the special police were involved in the burning of Donji Lapac." And your answer was: "No." Does that mean that, no, they were not involved in the burning of Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: That meant that, no, they were not involved in the burning of anything in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. Mr. Vitez, can you please -- having worked with General Markac over the years in the special police, can you please give the Chamber an idea of what kind of a person and the character of General Markac is.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I can provide the Trial Chamber with my personal view, since I have known General Markac since 1987, on -- or 1988. At that time, he was an instructor for physical training and self-defence. I know that he was always a very responsible person, perseverant person. There was no impossible task for him. There was nothing that could not be achieved. As a General and as a manager, he has always been held in very high esteem, and not only among the ranks of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Any need to question the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Waespi, to cross-examine the witness, I would like to seek clarification on one matter. Mr. Vitez, you said in the early stages when you had break through the first lines, you had asked for artillery support. Who gave that artillery support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The artillery support was provided by our special police support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it your own artillery unit attached to the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were support for everybody. They were independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was an artillery unit composed of members of the special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they would give support to -- if you say to everybody, what do I have to understand "everybody"? Being not only your police unit but also other police units? Or not only special police units but also other combat units outside the special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They provided support to the special police only. Not only to my unit, the unit that I was a member of. It all depended on where they were deployed and who was it who asked for support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did the special police, during this Velebit to Donji Lapac exercise, did they rely on any artillery support from any unit outside the special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know about my unit and about my axis prompts me to say no. I know for sure that that didn't happen where I was, but as for the rest of the units, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us that when you arrived Donji Lapac there was artillery fire, but you didn't know whether it was friendly fire or not. And you added to that, that you had not asked for artillery support at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We did not seek artillery support. When we arrived at the entrance to that hamlet, there was artillery fire. We were pounded. We had to halt and wait, and then we communicated a message to our support to find out who it was who was firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that on your axis you did not ask for any artillery support.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not engage at any point in time, and there was no need. The area was woody and rocky, and there was no need to ask for artillery support at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be true also for the passing through the villages you went through? Villages and towns. You said you arrived at Stikada. No need to have any artillery support there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My unit and our axis after Mali Alan, we never asked for artillery support, until the very end, including Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would include Gracac as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any impacts of artillery fire in Gracac during these first days of August? You told us that you had seen damaged buildings with vegetation already. But are you aware of any artillery impacts on Gracac during the days you were in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't see or witness such an artillery attack. When I entered Gracac, I did not see any artillery impacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was your units that liberated that area of Gracac, or were there any non-special police units involved in the liberation of Gracac and moving on to Bruvno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that time, I saw only members of the special police, nobody else, either during the liberation of Gracac or Bruvno. It was only in Lapac that I saw members of the Croatian Army for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said when you -- let me just check. One second. You earlier said your unit did not return to Gracac, but you said they returned to -- after you had finished, after you had completed your combat activities. I could try to find it. Could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we completed our operation, our unit returned to the territory of the Varazdin police administration. Our next action was to act as reserve in the mop-up operation on Mount Petrova Gora. After that, the unit went to the territory of Dubrovnik and Neretva county where we manned positions facing Montenegro. And we returned to that area sometime in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that your unit returned not through Gracac but through Udbina. Who chose the route of return, and do you have any idea what triggered to choose the Udbina route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The return route was chosen by the unit command. And why we went through Udbina, the reason was practical. It cut our journey by nearly 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Waespi, if there's any subject, we've still got seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I can start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vitez, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is it counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Vitez. I understand that you were the assistant commander of the Varazdin special police unit. And you referred to a commander a couple of times. Who was the name of that commander of the Varazdin special police unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: The commander of the special police unit in Varazdin was Mr. Ivica Mindek.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you spell his last name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: M-i-n-d-e-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And for how long was he the commander of the special police in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Ivica Mindek was our commander from 1993 to 1997, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vitez. And I take it that Mr. Mindek was then the author of the report from which we -- you read excerpts about the activities of the Varazdin unit.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was your exact function? Did you deputize your commander when he wasn't available? Did you have separate command functions? Did you go to meetings when Mr. Mindek couldn't go? Can you explain a little bit the relationship between the commander and you, as the assistant commander during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Our unit had two assistant commanders. I was one of them, and the other one was Mr. Horinec. My duty as an assistant commander was to work with instructors. Also to design various activities for the entire unit. Also to implement the training plan, the military and police tactics plans, as well as some other activities that we engaged in. The other assistant dealt with some of those matters as well. However, he was also involved and dealt with the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And your role specifically during Operation Storm was what? I take it you had no contacts with instructors or anybody else. Did you have a specific role, a specific combat role, or advisory role, or whatever? Can you enlighten me on that.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: In that operation, everything was the same as in other operations. Our reconnaissance squad went before the unit, and after them, the commander went with his two assistants in order to control and monitor the situation and developments in order to be able to lead the unit into combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these two assistants would be you and your -- your colleague?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were basically following the commander during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Well, we didn't only follow them. We were always there together with the entire unit, with those men who were breaking through, who were first. However, we were considered the most responsible ones in the unit and we never allowed ourselves to let our men go and tell them that we would follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just briefly before we adjourn, I understand from various documents that the unit was about 120 to 140 special policemen, your unit that came from Varazdin to Knin.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN VITEZ
utterances.text: Yes. There was some 100 active policemen, about 30 or so reserve policemen and the rest were men who had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just might be an error in the question that the unit came from Varazdin to Knin. I don't think there has been any --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, from Varazdin to the Zadar police administration for the first time on the 22nd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Going to -- preparing for going to Velebit. Yes, that's -- Then one final question from me, Mr. Vitez. Varazdin, is that north of Zagreb or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Varazdin is the northernmost city in Croatia. To our left is the Republic of Slovenia, and to our right is the Republic of Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Beautiful city, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi, perhaps after retirement. We adjourn for the day. Mr. Vitez, we would like to see you back tomorrow, not in the morning but in the afternoon. Because we adjourn and we will resume tomorrow -- Yes, I first have to instruct you - one second, please - I have to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony that you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, the 10th of December, at a quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in courtroom -- no, I make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- was confirmed that I didn't make a mistake. We resume tomorrow, the 10th of December, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of December, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
